note: HAND-WRITTEN plain-language descriptions, for a reader who has never encountered a substance and does not know what it is. PsychonautWiki cannot supply these: its `summary` field is a scraped warning box that is frequently junk ("Summary sheet: MDMA MDMA"), and its `effects` field returns only the substance's own name. Both were checked against the live API on 2026-08-10 before writing these by hand.
rules: Say what it IS and what people take it FOR. Someone who does not know cannot assess a warning about it.
No dosing, no route advice, no how-to. Dose ranges already live in their own section with their own caveats.
Neither advertise nor frighten. 'Euphoric' oversells; 'deadly poison' is the fear-based framing EVIDENCE.md rejects. Describe.
Name the ordinary medical use where there is one - most people meet oxycodone, ketamine and diazepam in a hospital first.
Plain words. Roughly an 8th-grade reading level, no pharmacology unless it changes what someone would do.

descriptions.alcohol: The drug in beer, wine and spirits. It slows the brain and body down, which is why it makes people relaxed and unsteady — and why it gets dangerous next to other things that slow you down, like opioids or benzos. It is legal and completely ordinary, and that is exactly why people forget it belongs on this list.
descriptions.cannabis: The dried flower of the cannabis plant, smoked, vaped or eaten. What it does varies a lot between people and between strains — usually relaxation, changed senses and hunger, though some people get anxiety or a racing heart instead. Eaten, it takes much longer to come on than smoked, and that is the single most common way people take more than they meant to.
descriptions.mdma: A stimulant that also does something to your feelings, sold as ecstasy or molly, in pills or powder. People take it for warmth, closeness and energy, mostly around other people and music. It pushes up your body temperature and heart rate. A lot of what gets sold under these names is not MDMA at all.
descriptions.lsd: A psychedelic, usually sold on small squares of blotter paper. It changes how you see, think and feel for a long time — eight to twelve hours is normal, which is far longer than most people expect the first time. It does not stop your breathing the way an opioid overdose does, but a bad one can be genuinely distressing, and how it goes depends a lot on your mood, who you are with and where you are.
descriptions.psilocybin-mushrooms: Mushrooms containing psilocybin, sometimes called magic mushrooms or shrooms, usually eaten dried or brewed into tea. You get visual changes, shifts in thinking and mood, and often strong emotion, for about four to six hours. The main physical danger is picking the wrong wild mushroom, not the psilocybin.
descriptions.ketamine: An anesthetic used in hospitals and by vets, also used as a powder to get high. It makes you feel detached from your body and your surroundings, and at higher amounts you can end up unable to move or respond at all — which is dangerous around vomiting, water, or being on your own. Using a lot, regularly, is strongly linked to serious bladder damage.
descriptions.cocaine: A stimulant made from the coca plant, sold as a white powder. It makes you alert, confident and full of energy for a short time — often under an hour — which is why people keep going back for more. It puts strain on the heart, and mixing it with alcohol makes your body create a third substance that is harder on the heart than either one alone.
descriptions.crack-cocaine: Cocaine cooked into a smokable rock. Same drug as powder, but smoking gets it there faster and it wears off sooner, so people redose more often and dependence builds more easily.
descriptions.heroin: An opioid made from morphine, sold as powder or sticky tar. It kills pain and brings warmth and heavy sedation. Across much of the US, what is sold as heroin now has fentanyl in it, or simply is fentanyl — which is why strength can change without warning from one batch to the next.
descriptions.fentanyl: A synthetic opioid used in hospitals for severe pain, and now the main opioid in the street supply. It works in far smaller amounts than heroin, so it is very hard to mix evenly — two scoops out of the same bag can be different strengths. It also turns up in drugs nobody sold as opioids at all.
descriptions.methamphetamine: A stimulant that lasts a long time, sold as crystals or powder. It keeps you alert, energetic and awake for many hours — much longer than cocaine. Using a lot of it, or using for a long time, is linked to losing sleep and weight, damage to your teeth, and paranoia or psychosis that can hang around after you stop.
descriptions.amphetamine: A stimulant, prescribed as Adderall for ADHD and also used without a prescription. It sharpens focus, gives you energy, keeps you awake and kills appetite. The prescribed and street versions are the same drug — the difference is that a prescription comes with a known strength.
descriptions.methylphenidate: A stimulant prescribed as Ritalin or Concerta, mostly for ADHD. It sharpens focus and gives you energy, and does not last as long as amphetamine.
descriptions.alprazolam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Xanax for anxiety and panic. It calms you, sedates you, and wipes your memory of the hours you were on it. Mixed with opioids or alcohol it is one of the most common things found in fatal overdoses, and pressed pills sold as Xanax very often contain something else entirely.
descriptions.diazepam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Valium for anxiety, muscle spasm and alcohol withdrawal. It lasts longer than most of its family. Stopping suddenly after using it regularly can cause seizures — it is one of the few drugs where quitting cold turkey is more dangerous than coming off slowly.
descriptions.oxycodone: An opioid painkiller, prescribed as OxyContin or Percocet. It kills pain, sedates you and brings euphoria. Pills sold as oxycodone outside a pharmacy — especially ones stamped M30 — are very often pressed fentanyl instead.
descriptions.codeine: A weaker opioid, in some prescription cough syrups and pain tablets. Your body turns it into morphine, and how much it turns varies a lot person to person — so the same tablet hits two people differently.
descriptions.buprenorphine: An opioid used to treat opioid dependence and pain, prescribed as Suboxone or Subutex. It sits on the same receptors without doing the same thing, which takes away withdrawal and cravings. Because it grips those receptors so tightly, taking it too soon after another opioid can throw you straight into withdrawal.
descriptions.tramadol: A prescription painkiller that works partly like a weak opioid and also messes with serotonin. That second part is why it reacts badly with antidepressants and raises the chance of a seizure — it does not behave like other opioids of similar strength.
descriptions.kratom: The leaf of a Southeast Asian tree, taken as powder, capsules or tea. Smaller amounts feel more like a stimulant, larger amounts more like a mild opioid. Some people use it for pain, or to get through opioid withdrawal. Using it regularly can build dependence, with a withdrawal of its own.
descriptions.ghb: A depressant sold as a salty liquid, used to get high and sometimes to sleep. Here is the thing that makes it dangerous: the amount that gets you high and the amount that knocks you out are very close together. Drink alcohol with it and that gap gets smaller still.
descriptions.dmt: A very short, very intense psychedelic, usually smoked or vaped. It arrives within seconds and is usually over in fifteen to thirty minutes. It is also what makes ayahuasca work — combined with an MAOI it lasts hours instead, and that combination reacts seriously with a lot of medications.
descriptions.mescaline: A psychedelic found in peyote, San Pedro and related cacti, used in Indigenous ceremony for a very long time. Visual and emotional changes lasting roughly ten to twelve hours. Peyote grows slowly and is under threat, and its ceremonial use is legally protected for members of the Native American Church.
descriptions.2c-b: A synthetic psychedelic with a stimulant edge, sold as pills or powder. Shorter than LSD — usually four to eight hours. It belongs to a family of near-identical chemicals with very different strengths, and mixing one up for another is the usual way people get hurt with it.
descriptions.nitrous: Nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, used by dentists and to charge whipped cream canisters. Breathed in, you get about a minute of dizziness and distortion. Two specific dangers: suffocating if you breathe it without oxygen, and nerve damage from using a lot of it, because it strips out your vitamin B12.
descriptions.pregabalin: A prescription medicine for nerve pain, seizures and anxiety, sold as Lyrica. It is a depressant and piles onto the sedation from opioids and alcohol, which is why it shows up in overdose reports far more often than its reputation would suggest.
descriptions.gabapentin: A prescription medicine for nerve pain and seizures, sold as Neurontin. Like pregabalin it sedates you and stacks with opioids and alcohol. People tend to assume it is harmless because it is everywhere and handed out freely.
descriptions.methadone: An opioid that lasts a long time, used both to treat opioid dependence and for pain. It outlasts heroin or fentanyl by a long way — often more than a day — which is what makes it good for holding off withdrawal, and also what makes it dangerous: it stacks up in your body over the first few days of taking it.
descriptions.morphine: The original opioid painkiller, made from the opium poppy and still used in hospitals for severe pain. Nearly every other opioid gets measured against it.
descriptions.hydrocodone: An opioid painkiller, prescribed as Vicodin or Norco, usually mixed with acetaminophen. That mix matters: taking extra tablets to get more opioid also means more acetaminophen, and acetaminophen wrecks your liver.
descriptions.hydromorphone: A strong opioid painkiller, prescribed as Dilaudid, used in hospitals for severe pain. A good deal stronger than morphine, milligram for milligram.
descriptions.oxymorphone: A strong opioid painkiller, prescribed as Opana. Stronger than oxycodone, milligram for milligram.
descriptions.tapentadol: A prescription painkiller that works as an opioid and also acts on norepinephrine. Like tramadol, that second action means it reacts with antidepressants in ways other opioids do not.
descriptions.pethidine: An older opioid painkiller, also called meperidine or Demerol, once common in childbirth and surgery. Used far less now, because something it breaks down into builds up with repeated doses and can cause seizures.
descriptions.dihydrocodeine: An opioid painkiller about as strong as codeine, found in some prescription tablets and cough medicines.
descriptions.o-desmethyltramadol: What your body turns tramadol into — and the part that actually kills the pain. It also gets sold on its own, sometimes in things marketed as herbal, which is a problem: you have no idea of the strength and it carries tramadol's seizure risk.
descriptions.dextropropoxyphene: An opioid painkiller pulled from the US and much of Europe because it caused heart rhythm problems and deaths at amounts not far above a normal dose.
descriptions.acetylfentanyl: A fentanyl analogue — a chemical cousin of fentanyl. It was never made as a medicine and turns up in the street opioid supply. Like fentanyl, it works in tiny amounts, so it is hard to mix evenly.
descriptions.sufentanil: A hospital opioid, used in surgery and epidurals. Far stronger than fentanyl for the same amount, with no safe margin outside a clinical setting.
descriptions.u-47700: A synthetic opioid, sometimes sold as pink or U4. It was made for research, never approved as a medicine, and shows up in the street supply as a powder or pressed into counterfeit pills.
descriptions.dextromethorphan: The cough suppressant in a lot of over-the-counter cold medicines, often labeled DXM. In larger amounts it works as a dissociative, leaving you detached and altering what you perceive. The real practical danger is cold medicines that also contain acetaminophen or antihistamines, which turn toxic long before the DXM wears off.
descriptions.pcp: A dissociative anesthetic, also called angel dust, dropped from medical use because of how confused and agitated people were as it wore off. It leaves you detached from your body and your surroundings, and does unpredictable things to mood and behavior.
descriptions.mephedrone: A stimulant, also called 4-MMC or meow meow, sold as powder or in capsules. Energy and sociability for a short time, which is exactly why people redose.
descriptions.3-mmc: A stimulant closely related to mephedrone, sold after mephedrone got banned in a lot of countries. Similar effects, similarly short.
descriptions.a-pvp: A stimulant that lasts a long time, sometimes called flakka, part of the cathinone family. Effects can run for many hours, and at higher amounts it brings agitation, sleeplessness and confusion.
descriptions.methylone: A stimulant with a mild emotional edge, chemically related to MDMA but much weaker on that front. It has been sold as MDMA, and mixed into things labeled MDMA.
descriptions.mda: A psychedelic stimulant closely related to MDMA, sometimes called sally. Lasts longer than MDMA, with more visual effect and less of the emotional warmth.
descriptions.mdea: A drug closely related to MDMA, sometimes called eve, with a milder emotional effect.
descriptions.gbl: A liquid solvent that your body turns into GHB, with the same effects and the same tiny gap between the amount that gets you high and the amount that knocks you out. It hits faster than GHB, which makes that gap even harder to judge.
descriptions.baclofen: A prescription muscle relaxant for spasticity, sometimes used for alcohol dependence. It is a depressant and adds to what opioids and alcohol are already doing. Stopping it suddenly after regular use can cause serious withdrawal.
descriptions.mdai: A drug related to MDMA that brings emotional warmth without much stimulation. Sometimes sold as a legal stand-in for MDMA.
descriptions.5-apb: A stimulant with a psychedelic edge, sold as an MDMA substitute, and often lasting a lot longer than people expect.
descriptions.6-apb: A stimulant with a psychedelic edge, sometimes called benzo fury, sold as an MDMA substitute. It comes on slowly — the usual way people end up taking more than they meant to — and then lasts a long time.
descriptions.caffeine: The stimulant in coffee, tea and energy drinks, and a very common cutting agent in powders sold as something else. On its own it is mild; mixed into a stimulant it makes a bag look bigger without making it stronger.
descriptions.nicotine: The drug in tobacco and vapes. It is a stimulant, it builds dependence fast, and concentrated vape liquid is genuinely dangerous to swallow — especially around children.
descriptions.clonazepam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Klonopin for seizures and panic. Long-acting. Like the rest of its family it stacks with opioids and alcohol, and stopping suddenly after regular use can cause seizures.
descriptions.lorazepam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Ativan for anxiety and seizures. Shorter-acting than diazepam. Same two rules as the rest of the family: it stacks dangerously with opioids and alcohol, and coming off it needs to be gradual.
descriptions.zolpidem: A sleeping pill, prescribed as Ambien. Not a benzodiazepine but it acts on the same system and carries the same danger next to opioids and alcohol. It is well known for people doing things while apparently awake and having no memory of it.
descriptions.zopiclone: A sleeping pill, sold as Imovane or Zimovane. Like zolpidem it is not a benzodiazepine but behaves like one, including how badly it mixes with opioids and alcohol. Often leaves a metallic taste.
descriptions.eszopiclone: A sleeping pill, prescribed as Lunesta. Closely related to zopiclone and carries the same warning about mixing with opioids or alcohol.
descriptions.etizolam: A benzodiazepine-type drug prescribed in a few countries and sold widely online everywhere else. It is often what is actually in a pill sold as Xanax. Strength varies enormously batch to batch, which is what makes it dangerous alongside opioids.
descriptions.flualprazolam: A designer benzodiazepine, never a medicine anywhere. It turns up pressed into counterfeit Xanax and is considerably stronger than alprazolam, so a pill that looks familiar can be far more sedating than expected.
descriptions.flubromazolam: A designer benzodiazepine, never approved as a medicine. Very strong in very small amounts and long-lasting, which is a bad combination when nobody knows how much is in a pill.
descriptions.metizolam: A designer benzodiazepine sold online, never a medicine. Like the others in this group, the real problem is that the amount in any given pill is unknown.
descriptions.deschloroetizolam: A designer benzodiazepine related to etizolam, never approved as a medicine and not made to any consistent strength.
descriptions.phenibut: A Russian anxiety medicine sold as a supplement in the US. It is a depressant and adds to alcohol and opioids. Dependence builds faster than people expect, and the withdrawal is genuinely severe — closer to benzodiazepine withdrawal than to a hangover.
descriptions.f-phenibut: A stronger, faster version of phenibut, sold as a supplement. Same dependence and same severe withdrawal, reached sooner.
descriptions.modafinil: A prescription wakefulness drug, sold as Provigil, used for narcolepsy and shift work. It keeps you awake without much of a stimulant rush. It speeds up how the liver clears some medicines, which matters most for hormonal birth control.
descriptions.armodafinil: A longer-lasting version of modafinil, prescribed as Nuvigil, with the same effects and the same interaction with hormonal birth control.
descriptions.psilocin: What your body turns psilocybin into, and the part that actually does something. It is also what is measured when mushrooms are tested.
descriptions.datura: A plant — jimsonweed or thornapple — containing deliriants. This is not a psychedelic: people experience convincing hallucinations they cannot tell from real, often with no memory afterwards. The amount varies wildly between plants and even between parts of the same plant, and the gap between an active and a poisonous dose is small.
descriptions.ayahuasca: A brew from South America combining a DMT-containing plant with an MAOI plant, traditionally used in ceremony. The MAOI is what makes it last hours rather than minutes, and it is also the part that reacts dangerously with many antidepressants and with some foods.
descriptions.changa: DMT absorbed onto an herb blend that includes an MAOI, made to be smoked. It lasts longer than smoked DMT alone, and the MAOI brings the same medication interactions ayahuasca has.
